title: Beyond All Inclusive: An Exploration of Resort Hotel Guests’ Perceived Value of “Ultra All-Inclusive” Package Additions
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Beyond All Inclusive: An Exploration of Resort Hotel Guests’ Perceived Value of “Ultra All-Inclusive” Package Additions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial or personal conflicts of interest related to the research or its findings. The work was conducted independently without influence from commercial entities, hospitality suppliers, tour operators, or resort brands.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The study involved anonymous volunteer participants and collected no personally identifiable information. Written consent was obtained from all respondents prior to participation. Formal ethics committee approval was not required as no personal or sensitive data were collected.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The study was conducted independently by the author as part of a personal research project originating from and following after an MBA dissertation.

detail.abstract:
This study examines the perceived value of package elements that extend beyond standard All-Inclusive (AI) offers, focusing on the emerging Ultra All-Inclusive (Ultra AI) resort model. To support more effective package design and pricing decisions, a two-stage, multi-method approach was employed. First, content analysis of over 400 Ultra AI package descriptions was conducted to identify current practices and reveal performance drivers through analysis of Tripadvisor’s “Top 25” AI hotels. Second, an online survey of 141 resort guests measured perceived value and willingness-to-accept higher prices (WTA) for 52 non-standard package inclusions.
The findings highlight the dominance of Food & Beverage (F&B) offerings in driving both satisfaction and positive electronic word-of-mouth (e-WOM), while revealing a high implied willingness-to-pay for uncommon but emerging inclusions such as Dine-out experiences, spa sessions, no check in/out times and at least one included excursion. Suggested innovations emerging from guest responses signal opportunities for further development of the Ultra AI model.
The study contributes to the limited literature on Ultra AI tourism by synthesizing stated guest value with revealed performance indicators, offering actionable insights for resort managers and hoteliers.

title: Buyer Platform Experience (PLX) in Online Marketplaces: Scale Development, Validation, and the Salience of Variety, Competitive Pricing, Service Excellence, and Promotion
affiliations: Antalya Bilim University, Istanbul Commerce University, Istanbul Commerce University, Istanbul Commerce University and Antalya Bilim University

detail.title: Buyer Platform Experience (PLX) in Online Marketplaces: Scale Development, Validation, and the Salience of Variety, Competitive Pricing, Service Excellence, and Promotion
detail.abstract: This study aims to develop and validate a Buyer Platform Experience (PLX) scale focused on the cognitive and relational dimensions of buyer experience in online marketplaces. Adopting a five-stage sequential scale-development methodology, the research combines qualitative interviews with quantitative analyses using SPSS and AMOS. A four-dimensional scale-variety, service excellence, competitive pricing, and promotional effectiveness-was validated through exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses. Structural equation modeling confirmed that variety, service excellence, and competitive pricing significantly predict customer loyalty. The findings isolate cognitive and relational aspects often overlooked in existing customerexperience frameworks and offer practical guidance for platform managers seeking to enhance buyer retention through service quality, price competitiveness, and variety management.

title: A Study on Tam in Grocery Apps in India
affiliations: Vivekananda Institute of Professional Studies-Technical Campus,  and NDIM - New Delhi Institute of Management

detail.title: A Study on Tam in Grocery Apps in India
detail.abstract: Present study is to know Technology acceptance model (TAM) in grocery apps in Indian scenario. Variables used for the study are Perceived usefulness in grocery apps, Perceived ease of use Behavioral Intentions to use grocery mobile apps and Actual use of Grocery mobile apps. Primary data is collected from users of grocery apps in India using structured questionnaire on interval data. Study of period is 2022. TAM model in grocery apps proves that there is significant association among Perceived usefulness in grocery apps, Perceived ease of use, Behavioral Intentions to use grocery mobile apps and Actual use of Grocery mobile apps. Limitation of the study is that in future period perception on TAM model may vary. Future scope of the study is that Indian market can be studied with respect to rural areasfor research as rural market is still untapped.

title: "Frictionless" Future: How Free Small Payments can Propel the Growth of Data-based Decision Making
affiliations: Woxsen University and Woxsen University

detail.title: "Frictionless" Future: How Free Small Payments can Propel the Growth of Data-based Decision Making

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This Reserach work is not finded by any third party or organization
declarations.funderStatement: This Reserach work is not finded by any third party or organization

detail.abstract: Today technical revolution has emerged global power, which is empowering digital transactions more accessible and accurate in India. The Indian digital payments market is now valued at approximately $85 billion, with the CAGR of 23% over the past five years and is projected to reach $135 billion by 2027. Most of these digital payments (95%) are Small in value. At this point with the government policies advancement, businesses are using Small Payments data to understand and analyze consumer behavior and its insights adopted for data-based decisionmaking processes by promoting financial inclusion and reshaping transactions practices.

title: Exploring Unique Marketing Paradigm -"NeuroMarketing: Today and Tomorrow"
affiliations: Vivekananda Institute of Professional Studies-Technical Campus and Vivekananda Institute of Professional Studies-Technical Campus

detail.title: Exploring Unique Marketing Paradigm -"NeuroMarketing: Today and Tomorrow"
detail.abstract: The modern age of fundamental marketing is creating an information age. Gone are those days when the primary concern of businesses was large production and mass consumption, where the stores were full with inventory and presented the customers with a wild discount. The emergence of modern information technology has made everything within reach for the consumers to compare their preferences with the competitors only a click away. Marketing is not all about selling a product or reaching out to customers but about making a trustworthy and loyal relationship along with customer satisfaction by creating an impressive product. The neuromarketing technique has paved the way for a new age of marketing where more research and studies are being conducted to know the consumers in detail. Neuromarketing is an emerging discipline in the area of marketing and social science research representing an amalgamation of three popular disciplines; Psychology, Marketing, and Neuroscience. Neuromarketing offers a deeper understanding of consumer thought processes deriving out of the subconscious mind which is beyond the scope of traditional methods of marketing. While the traditional forms of marketing only explain how a consumer responds to marketing stimuli, neuromarketing answers both the “how” and “why” aspects of consumer behaviour. This paper introduces the readers to this emerging yet unexplored field of marketing by highlighting its evolution, techniques, and scope in the real world. Further, the study brings forward the ethical concerns faced in the application of neuroscientific techniques for the study of consumer behaviour. The review highlights the concept as a significant contribution to the field of marketing which helps in examining the brain and other activities of the human body. However, the lack of privacy, trust, and harm associated with the use of neuroscientific techniques raise serious concerns about its application.

title: A study on the mechanism of digital literacy enhancement among rural women based on dynamic capability theory-evidence from the Broadband-China strategy
affiliations: Chongqing Normal University and Chongqing Normal University

detail.title: A study on the mechanism of digital literacy enhancement among rural women based on dynamic capability theory-evidence from the Broadband-China strategy
detail.abstract: Against the backdrop of rapid digital economic development, enhancing rural women's digital literacy holds significant strategic importance for promoting gender equality and advancing sustainable rural development. Drawing upon dynamic capability theory, this study constructs a theoretical analytical framework encompassing three dimensions-opportunity perception-learning absorption-resource restructuring-to systematically elucidate the formation mechanism of rural women's digital literacy. Utilizing data from the China Family Panel Studies (CFPS) spanning 2014–2020, the study treats the phased implementation of the “Broadband China” strategy at the county level as a quasi-natural experiment. A multi-period double difference model is employed for causal identification. Empirical results indicate that the Broadband-China strategy significantly enhances rural women's digital literacy, with policy effects exhibiting notable heterogeneity across marital status, educational attainment, and regional dimensions. Mechanism tests reveal two primary pathways: learning absorption through increased reliance on internet information channels, and resource restructuring via expanded social networks. This validates the explanatory power of the dynamic capabilities framework. This study not only offers new analytical perspectives on how digital infrastructure influences individual capability development but also provides crucial empirical evidence for advancing digital inclusion and designing targeted rural digital policies.

title: Credit expansion and countercyclical bank equity issuance: evidence from China
affiliations: Shanghai Lixin Univeristy of Accounting and Finance, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Xiamen University - Department of Finance and Shanghai Lixin University of Accounting and Finance

detail.title: Credit expansion and countercyclical bank equity issuance: evidence from China
detail.abstract: This paper examines how broad credit expansion shapes banks’ external equity financing in a large, heterogeneous emerging-market banking system. Using a parsimonious two-sector DSGE framework and an annual panel of China’s A-share listed commercial banks (2007–2023), the analysis shows that credit booms significantly suppress equity issuance—an effect that is economically larger for big, state-influenced banks. Mechanism tests indicate the countercyclical pattern operates mainly through three channels: reductions in investment valuation (Tobin’s Q), mechanically higher leverage ratios, and increased internally generated cash flows, each of which lowers the marginal incentive to issue new equity. Institutional features moderate these dynamics: expectations of official bailouts, greater state ownership, the introduction of deposit insurance, and dual listing arrangements amplify the negative relation, whereas higher expected credit risk and more costly debt financing attenuate it. The procyclicality extends beyond ordinary equity to hybrid Tier-1 instruments (e.g., perpetual bonds). Results are robust to dynamic panels, SUR/IV approaches, and alternative financing measures. The paper contributes a unified theoretical account and comprehensive empirical evidence on equity issuance cyclicality in an emerging market, and recommends differentiated, risk-sensitive countercyclical capital buffers, reforms to depositor-protection design, and deeper market-based capital channels to mitigate cyclicality while preserving credit provision.

title: In Algorithms We Trust? Public Experience, Trust, and Attitudes Toward Responsible AI in Local Government
affiliations: Queensland University of Technology, Queensland University of Technology, City University of Hong Kong (CityU), Islamic University of Madinah and Queensland University of Technology

detail.title: In Algorithms We Trust? Public Experience, Trust, and Attitudes Toward Responsible AI in Local Government
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in local government operations, transforming public service delivery while raising complex questions of trust and responsibility. Local governments, as the institutions closest to citizens’ daily lives, must balance technological innovation with community values and ethical expectations. This research examines how citizens’ experience, understanding, and trust shape perceptions of AI in local governance and influence support for responsible AI principles. Drawing on survey data from 1,183 respondents across Australia, Hong Kong, and Saudi Arabia, the analysis employs structural equation modelling to test an “exposure to ethics” framework that links experience, understanding, trust, perceived risks and benefits, attitudes toward urban and surveillance AI applications and the prioritisation of responsible AI. Results show that experience enhances understanding, which fosters trust and anchors perceptions of benefit and positive attitudes of AI in public services. Positive experiences with visible urban AI extend to broader acceptance of more contested technologies such as surveillance. Across contexts, public prioritisation of responsible AI is shaped more by risk awareness than benefit recognition. Cross-national comparisons highlight how governance traditions and demographic structures moderate these dynamics: Australia reflects risk-sensitive accountability norms, Hong Kong emphasises experiential trust, and Saudi Arabia demonstrates institutionally anchored confidence. This research contributes a comparative model for understanding how experiential familiarity, public trust, and ethical expectations interact in shaping responsible AI governance at the municipal level, emphasising the importance of inclusive and context-sensitive governance.

title: Easy Money, Easy Spending: Evidence from Commodity Export Windfalls
affiliations: Center for Natural Resource Studies (CNRS), University of Oxford and Washington University in St. Louis

detail.title: Easy Money, Easy Spending: Evidence from Commodity Export Windfalls
detail.abstract: When wealth or income rises suddenly, the propensity for that “easy money” to be directed towards unproductive use, “easy spending”, may rise. The cross-country relationship between conspicuous consumption and revenue windfalls is explored by estimating the response of demand for imports of luxury goods resulting from country-specific and plausibly exogenous variation in commodity export prices. The response of imports of luxury goods following a commodity export windfall is found to be bigger than that for non-luxury imports while there is substantial heterogeneity in the magnitude of the response between different categories of luxury import goods. The results also point to a significant increase in tourism from countries experiencing commodity export windfalls to the main luxury shopping destinations abroad. Countries that have higher inequality, weaker control of corruption or  democracy have significantly higher luxury import response following a commodity export windfall. These results provide a novel channel of the resource curse.

title: DRE-YOLO: A dual-path retinex enhancement network for low-light object detection
affiliations: South China University of Technology and South China University of Technology

detail.title: DRE-YOLO: A dual-path retinex enhancement network for low-light object detection
detail.abstract: Low-light and uneven illumination conditions often degrade the performance of existing object detectors, resulting in compromised accuracy and limited real-time capability. To address these issues, we propose DRE-YOLO, an efficient end-to-end low-light detector that integrates a dual-path retinex enhancement (DRE) network with the YOLOv3 detector. First, our approach uses a retinex decomposition network to decompose the input image into reflectance and illumination components  based on the retinex theory. Subsequently, two dedicated modules are introduced to enhance the two components respectively.For reflectance component, we design the Reflectance Feature Boosting (RFB) module to enhance semantic features through multi-scale fusion and cross attention mechanisms. For illumination component, we propose the Illumination Adaptive Blance (IAB) module that leverages dual-branch attention channels to adjust illumination. The two refined components are recombined to generate enhanced images for detection. Trained with joint reconstruction and detection losses, we evaluate our method on the ExDark and DarkFace datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that our DRE-YOLO achieves superior performance and surpasses existing low-light object detection methods.

title: AI-Driven Transformation and the Reconfiguration of Competitiveness in Incumbent Firms
affiliations: Universidad Nebrija

detail.title: AI-Driven Transformation and the Reconfiguration of Competitiveness in Incumbent Firms
detail.abstract: This study investigates how Artificial Intelligence (AI) reshapes the strategic foundations of competitiveness in incumbent firms. Drawing on a comparative process-tracing analysis of five multinational corporations (2016–2025), the research reconstructs how AI-related capabilities evolve from efficiency-oriented applications to forms of anticipatory coordination that transform organizational learning, strategic decision-making, and value creation. Across cases, algorithmic infrastructures initially enhance operational performance but progressively become embedded in simulation, scenario exploration, and long-term interpretive routines. These developments reconfigure firms as hybrid socio-technical systems that construct and act upon model-based representations of possible futures. The findings identify common patterns in how learning trajectories, anticipatory practices, and ecosystem-level architectures emerge and interact, offering a theory-building contribution to understanding strategic adaptation in AI-intensive environments. The study outlines implications for long-range strategy, organizational foresight, and the governance of predictive systems, and proposes avenues for future research on distributed intelligence and learning architectures.

title: Private Equity and Creative Destruction: Evidence from the U.S. Power Sector

detail.title: Private Equity and Creative Destruction: Evidence from the U.S. Power Sector
detail.abstract: I study whether private equity (PE) owners facilitate creative destruction in the U.S. power generation sector by reallocating capital from inefficient to more efficient assets. Using the shale gas boom and the staggered expansion of natural gas pipelines as plausibly exogenous shocks that reduced the economic viability of coal and oil plants, I find that PE-owned plants are significantly more likely to be retired once they become uneconomic. In contrast, traditional utilities and local power producers are slower to exit because they face political and social frictions, such as labor opposition and reputational concerns, that impede shutdowns. Financial owners are less exposed to these nonpecuniary pressures and respond more readily to market signals. These results suggest that social and environmental protections, while well-intentioned, can inadvertently slow efficient exit and that PE ownership can mitigate these frictions and improve allocative efficiency.

title: Beyond Brown: Oil Shocks and Carbon Premium
affiliations: Tsinghua University and The Ohio State University

detail.title: Beyond Brown: Oil Shocks and Carbon Premium
detail.abstract: This paper reassesses the "carbon premium'', the higher cost of capital for carbon-intensive firms, by showing it is substantially confounded by oil shocks. Energy firms, the largest component of “brown” portfolios, have risk exposures and financing costs that move directly with oil shocks, unlike non-energy brown firms that primarily pass through input costs. These oil-specific shocks explain nearly half the carbon premium's variation during volatile periods. Re-examining the 2015 landmark Paris Agreement, we show that the documented post-PA carbon-premium increase in prior studies is entirely driven by the energy sector’s response to oil price dynamics, not carbon-transition risk.

title: C–SLO: Carbon–and SLO–Aware Global Load Balancing for Online Services
affiliations: University of Kalyani, University of Kalyani, University of Kalyani and Bengal College of Engineering and Technology

detail.title: C–SLO: Carbon–and SLO–Aware Global Load Balancing for Online Services
detail.abstract: International online platforms operate over significant distances where the carbon output of generated modular electricity and the associated service quality fluctuate. Left unbalanced, routing decisions made on latency alone result in an unexploited opportunity to save on carbon emissions, while uncoordinated routing decisions made with only carbon emissions in mind may entail the crossing of service level obligations (SLOs). Here we propose a global load-balancing policy, CSLO, which retains deployability alongside a focus on carbon reduction, while unavoidably treating latency and availability as hard constraints. We propose a model of routing as online constrained optimization on the probability simplex, and with a conservative primal–dual control design incorporating a trust region, SLO sentinels, and instant rollback. The distributed carbon-saturated communications controller receives real-time carbon emissions signals and serves telemetry, updates regional weights to change at short epochs, and executes proportional realizations of regional weight on commodity layer-7 proxies through connection draining in order to avoid service disruption. We provide the mathematical formulation, system design, and an assessment that incorporates strong baselines, ablations, and sensitivity to forecast error. In a realistic multi-regional replay, C-SLO demonstrates a reduction of tail latency in SLO-definite bounds. The manuscript includes design and result diagrams preanalysed in mathematical discourse alongside carbon emissions datasets leading to transparent scrutiny through the selection as well as outcomes of design choices.

title: The Evolution of Organizational Models in the Express Delivery Industry: An Inframarginal Analysis from the Perspective of Information Service
affiliations: Shandong University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: The Evolution of Organizational Models in the Express Delivery Industry: An Inframarginal Analysis from the Perspective of Information Service
detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of e-commerce has intensified the interdependence between digital platforms and express delivery firms, making information services a critical driver of logistics performance and organizational design. This study develops an inframarginal general equilibrium model to examine how improvements in information service capability, transaction efficiency, and the volume of tradable digital information shape the organizational evolution of the express delivery industry. We analyze four organizational modes: self-sufficiency, complete specialization, partial integration, and vertical integration. The results reveal that the emergence of independent information service providers is driven by scalable digital value-added capabilities, while rising information transaction costs encourage express firms to pursue varying degrees of integration with platforms. Moreover, when information service productivity outpaces logistics productivity, full vertical integration becomes the dominant equilibrium. Motivated by the development of China’s platform-based express delivery ecosystem, the model provides theoretical explanations for real-world patterns such as platform–logistics alliances and the rise of fully integrated e-commerce logistics systems. The findings offer actionable insights for platform operators, logistics firms, and policymakers seeking to optimize digital coordination, reduce transaction frictions, and design efficient e-commerce supply-chain structures.

title: The Ripple Effect: How CSR Propounds Brand Evangelism via eWOM, Altruism, and Affective Commitment Amid Customer Skepticism
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Prince Mohammad Bin Fahd University, affiliation not provided to SSRN and International University for Science & Technology

detail.title: The Ripple Effect: How CSR Propounds Brand Evangelism via eWOM, Altruism, and Affective Commitment Amid Customer Skepticism
detail.abstract: Corporate social responsibility (CSR) has long been recognised as a facilitator for positive customer behaviour, yet its role in promoting brand evangelism remains underexplored. This study develops and tests a moderated mediation model, grounded in social identity theory and relationship marketing theory, to uncover the psychological pathways through which CSR drives evangelism. Drawing on survey data from 332 telecom customers in India, the findings reveal that CSR stimulates electronic word-of-mouth (eWOM), which subsequently fosters affective commitment (AC) and altruism (AL). These relational mechanisms act as bridges linking CSR to brand evangelism (BE). Interestingly, CSR also propounds an insignificant impact on altruism (AL) and altruism (AL) does not act as the predecessor of brand evangelism (BE). CSR exerts negative direct effects on AC and BE, suggesting that its influence on advocacy is largely indirect. Moreover, customer skepticism weakens the CSR–eWOM relationship, underscoring critical boundary conditions for CSR effectiveness. Using structural equation modeling in SmartPLS 4, this study advances CSR and consumer psychology research by clarifying how prosocial brand initiatives translate into evangelistic behaviours and identifying the psychological levers that transform customers into passionate brand advocates.

title: Synergistic Learning from Demonstration for Complex Fabric Manipulation
affiliations: Wuhan Textile University

detail.title: Synergistic Learning from Demonstration for Complex Fabric Manipulation
detail.abstract: Automated fabric manipulation represents a critical challenge in garment manufacturing and logistics, where tasks such as folding and placement require handling high-dimensional deformable states with sparse feedback signals. Existing learning from demonstration methods optimize individual algorithmic components in isolation, resulting in limited performance on complex manipulation scenarios that require coordinated optimization of sampling efficiency, reward guidance, and training stability. To address this challenge, we present SynFM (Synergistic Fabric Manipulation), a coordinated component optimization framework that integrates prioritized experience replay, progress-aware reward engineering, and enhanced network architectures. The framework coordinates these components based on task complexity: prioritized sampling focuses on high-value transitions while structured rewards prevent unproductive exploration, and stabilized architectures maintain training robustness under aggressive sampling. Evaluation across four manipulation tasks shows substantial improvements, with success rates reaching 69\% on cloth folding and 95\% on rope straightening compared to 41\% and 72\% for existing methods, while reducing training variance by 63\% on complex tasks. Real-world deployment on a UR5 platform with RGB-D perception achieves comparable performance on cloth folding without task-specific calibration. The approach demonstrates that coordinated component optimization can improve learning efficiency and consistency for fabric manipulation, supporting automation in garment assembly and material handling applications.

title: Satellite Data Processing and Applications Using Cloud Computing: A Scalable and Efficient Approach
affiliations: University of Kalyani, University of Kalyani, University of Kalyani and Bengal College of Engineering and Technology

detail.title: Satellite Data Processing and Applications Using Cloud Computing: A Scalable and Efficient Approach
detail.abstract: At present, satellites are pivotal in tracking, climate monitoring, disaster assistance, and worldwide communication, however, the rapid expansion in sensor resolution and mission repetition has led to record-breaking divisions of unprocessed info. Conventional ground infrastructures, bound by limited storage space and processing capacity, tend to be incapable of providing the responsiveness modern applications demand. Cloud computing provides a successful alternative using elastic storage, distributed computation, and world-wide accessibility via AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. This paper focuses on how to unify satellite data systems with cloud environments, presenting a modular structure that includes scalable ingestion systems, real-time processing, and advanced security features.Taking the case study of weather satellite data, the model shown shows a processing speed up to 60% and cost savings of 30–45% over on-premises systems. Outside technology advantages, there are implications the research identifies for disaster recovery, agriculture, and joint research from the use of cloud computing. The conclusion section defines the future areas for investigation such as hybrid cloud-edge integration, automation based on artificial intelligence, and green cloud infrastructures.

title: Monetary Policy, Household Debt, and Heterogeneity in Canada: Bank-Level Analysis of Total Deposits
affiliations: Université de Moncton and Université de Moncton

detail.title: Monetary Policy, Household Debt, and Heterogeneity in Canada: Bank-Level Analysis of Total Deposits
detail.abstract: This paper examines how monetary policy, inflation, and household debt shape bank-level deposit dynamics in Canada from 2014 to 2022, a period encompassing the COVID-19 liquidity shock. While traditional studies of monetary transmission emphasize the credit channel, this research highlights the deposit channel as an active and heterogeneous mechanism. Using quarterly data from 34 federally regulated institutions and a dynamic panel System GMM estimator, the analysis explores how macroeconomic shocks interact with total bank deposits, accounting for differences in listing status and regulatory classification. Results indicate that real interest rates exert only a marginal influence on deposit accumulation, reflecting the persistence of low or negative real yields during the period. Nominal interest rates display a negative relationship with deposits, which turns positive when interacted with household indebtedness, while inflation erodes deposit growth. These findings reveal that high household leverage conditions the effectiveness of the deposit channel by weakening conventional saving responses. Heterogeneous effects across larger, listed institutions and smaller, non-systemically important banks further underscore the uneven dependence of financial intermediation on deposit dynamics. The results hold both academic and policy relevance, offering guidance to the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) in monitoring deposit resilience amid economic fluctuations.

title: Digital Capabilities, Behavioural Resilience, and Financial Inclusion in AI-Enabled Commerce: Evidence from Malaysia and Indonesia
affiliations: Universiti Putra Malaysia, Sebelas Maret University, Universiti Malaya, Universiti Putra Malaysia, Sebelas Maret University - Department of Economics Education, Bank Indonesia and Universitas Sebelas Maret

detail.title: Digital Capabilities, Behavioural Resilience, and Financial Inclusion in AI-Enabled Commerce: Evidence from Malaysia and Indonesia
detail.abstract: Digital financial services have become a core layer of AI-mediated commerce platforms, enabling individuals to transact, save, invest, and access financial tools within increasingly automated digital environments. However, meaningful participation in these ecosystems depends on the interaction of multiple digital capabilities and behavioural mechanisms, which remain uneven across emerging economies. This study proposes the Behavioural–Capability Model of FinTech Empowerment (BCMFE) to examine how AI literacy, financial literacy, digital financial literacy, FinTech adoption, and financial resilience jointly shape platform engagement in Malaysia and Indonesia. Using survey data from 1,150 participants and applying Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) with Multi-Group Analysis (MGA), the study identifies key capability–behaviour pathways across two distinct digital commerce contexts. The findings reveal that digital financial literacy and platform adoption behaviour are the strongest predictors of user participation, whereas AI literacy demonstrates asymmetric effects—neutral in Malaysia but negative in Indonesia—reflecting differences in perceived risk, trust in automation, and regulatory safeguards. Financial resilience further enhances platform engagement, functioning as a behavioural capability that supports sustained usage under uncertainty. Overall, the study advances electronic commerce research by integrating digital capabilities and behavioural resilience into a unified model, offering new insights into how users navigate AI-driven financial platforms in emerging economies.

title: Defining Three-Dimensional Warehouse: Transition from Two-Dimensional to Three-Dimensional Warehouse Automation with Digital Twin Integration
affiliations: Shantilal Shah Engineering College

detail.title: Defining Three-Dimensional Warehouse: Transition from Two-Dimensional to Three-Dimensional Warehouse Automation with Digital Twin Integration
detail.abstract: Traditional 2D warehouses are limited by poor space utilization and scalability, as they rely solely on horizontal expansion while neglecting vertical capacity. The term 3D warehouse has appeared only once in a recent preprint on AGV path planning, but is used descriptively without definition.  By conducting a systematic academic search across leading databases and journals, including Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, Taylor & Francis, ONOS (One Nation One Subscription) portal, Google Scholar and Wiley Online Libraryconfirmed that the term hasnot been formally defined or established. In this study, we formally define the 3D warehouse as an automated storage and retrieval system (AS/RS) system that fully exploits cubic storage space using robotic systems such as drones, shuttles, lifts and flexible automated guided vehicles (AGVs). This study also compares the four types of layouts, (i) traditional static 2D racks, (ii) shuttle-based 3D racks, (iii) cube-based dense storage systems and (iv) hybrid configurations, in simulation software for real-time performance optimisation. Key performance indicators (KPIs) such as throughput, cycle time, AGV utilization and storage density were analysed. Results show that digital twin-enabled hybrid warehouses outperform 2D layouts, reduce cycle times up to 60% and improve throughput by over 70%. The findings establish the hybrid warehouse as a novel perspective in logistics automation, providing a foundation for future research and adoption in Industry 4.0 environments. It also encourages a paradigm shift toward recognising and formally defining the 3D warehouse as a distinct class of automated logistics system.

title: Explainable AI–Driven Recommender Systems in E-Commerce: Effects on User Trust, Perceived Transparency, and Purchase Decisions
affiliations: Presidency University

detail.title: Explainable AI–Driven Recommender Systems in E-Commerce: Effects on User Trust, Perceived Transparency, and Purchase Decisions
detail.abstract: The opacity of artificial intelligence models in e-commerce recommender systems often creates a persistent “black box” problem that limits users’ ability to understand how recommendations are generated. This study examines how explainable AI (XAI) features influence user trust, perceived transparency, and purchase decisions. A mixed-methods approach was employed, combining a controlled between-subjects online experiment (n = 450) with semi-structured interviews (n = 30). Participants interacted with either a standard recommender system or an XAI-enhanced version that provided concise contextual explanations (e.g., “This recommendation is generated based on your recent viewing history”). Results show that XAI significantly increased user trust (M = 4.1 vs. 3.2, p < .001) and perceived transparency (M = 4.3 vs. 2.9, p < .001). Purchase rates were also higher in the XAI condition (68% vs. 49%), supported by a statistically significant group difference (χ² = 9.75, p = .002, OR = 2.19). Mediation analysis further demonstrated that trust and perceived transparency fully mediated the relationship between XAI exposure and purchase decisions. Qualitative insights reinforced these findings by showing that explanations reduced uncertainty and improved perceived credibility. Overall, this study provides empirical evidence of how XAI fosters user confidence and drives meaningful behavioral outcomes in e-commerce environments.

title: Value creation through disruptive technologies to mitigate complaints in last-mile deliveries during crisis
affiliations: Sheffield Hallam University, University of Sussex Business School and Clemson University

detail.title: Value creation through disruptive technologies to mitigate complaints in last-mile deliveries during crisis
detail.abstract: Global and regional crises have increasingly disrupted logistics and supply chain operations, exposing structural weaknesses in supply chains and testing strategic resilience of companies. Among these, last-mile delivery (LMD) services have become a critical determinant of customer satisfaction and competitive advantage in e-commerce. Although operational inefficiencies and customer dissatisfaction intensify during crisis, customer complaints about LMD performance remain underexplored in strategic management research. This study examines how disruptive technologies enable value creation and operational adaptation in LMD systems during and after crisis periods. Using secondary data from real customer complaints in Turkey and primary data from semi-structured interviews with senior managers of major LMD companies, the research employs qualitative content analysis to identify key service deficiencies and strategic responses. The analysis integrates Expectation–Confirmation Theory (ECT) and Process Theory (PT) to explain how firms transform technological adoption into value creation mechanisms that enhance service visibility, coordination, and reliability. Findings show that companies leveraging disruptive technologies (e.g., IoT, AI, BDA, Blockchain, Digital Twins, AR/VR, Cloud Computing, 5G, drones, and robotics) achieved significant reduction in customer complaints and improved process excellence in terms of visibility, coordination, and reliability. The study contributes to strategic management literature by linking technological innovation with strategic resilience and customer value creation in LMD contexts. It also provides managerial insights for developing adaptive technology strategies to improve last-mile competitiveness under uncertain and crisis conditions.

title: AI-Based Energy Consumption Forecasting in Smart Homes Using Multi-Algorithm Analysis Across Temporal Resolutions
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: AI-Based Energy Consumption Forecasting in Smart Homes Using Multi-Algorithm Analysis Across Temporal Resolutions
detail.abstract: The rising demand for electricity necessitates the development of advanced predictive models to enable effective load management and promote sustainable energy usage. In smart home applications, real-time monitoring and optimization of appliance-level energy consumption are crucial for enhancing energy efficiency. The proposed study analyses residential electricity usage patterns and forecasts appliance specific energy consumption using artificial intelligence (AI) techniques. A comprehensive evaluation involving ten machine learning algorithms was conducted to predict energy consumption across various time intervals such as hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, and quarterly. The objective is to identify the most suitable algorithm for each time frame to enhance energy optimization and scheduling. The analysis was implemented using Python on the Google Colab platform, and model performance was assessed using standard evaluation metrics such as Mean Squared Error (MSE), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), R-squared, and accuracy. The results revealed that the performance of forecasting models varies depending on the time interval. For hourly forecasts, a time series model achieved an accuracy of 99.96%. Daily predictions using the GBM + Optima model reached 95.63% accuracy. Weekly forecasts with the XGBoost model achieved 98.34% accuracy, while monthly and quarterly predictions using the NGBoost model reached 99.76% and 99.99% accuracy, respectively. These findings provide valuable insights for energy planners and homeowners to optimize electricity consumption. In conclusion, this research demonstrates the effectiveness of AI-based time series forecasting in managing residential energy usage and promoting efficient energy consumption practices.

title: Assessing the Readiness of Selected Departments at Al-Baha University to Integrate Artificial Intelligence Applications in E-Learning
affiliations: Albaha University

detail.title: Assessing the Readiness of Selected Departments at Al-Baha University to Integrate Artificial Intelligence Applications in E-Learning
detail.abstract: This study aimed to identify the extent to which selected academic departments in Al-Baha University are prepared to utilize Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications in e-learning. To achieve this objective, the descriptive approach was used, and data were collected through an electronic questionnaire distributed to a random sample consisting of 95 faculty members in three departments: the Biology Department at the Faculty of Science, Educational Technology Department at the Faculty of Education, and Family and Community Medicine Department at the Faculty of Medicine, and also 53 staff members of the E-learning Deanship. The findings revealed that the staff members at the deanship assessed the current implementation of e-learning practices as high, while their assessment of the departments’ ability to integrate AI applications in e-learning was rated as moderate. Meanwhile, faculty members’ assessments of their own scientific background in AI were also rated as moderate, yet their assessments of their readiness to use AI applications in e-learning were rated as high. Finally, the results revealed that faculty members at Al-Baha University strongly agreed on the existence of several obstacles that hinder the employment of AI applications in e-learning. The study identified key obstacles, such as limited training opportunities and insufficient infrastructure, and proposed strategic recommendations to address these gaps.

title: A Regulatory-Driven Planning Framework for Fast Charging Station Deployment in Power Distribution Systems
affiliations: Iran University of Science and Technology, Isfahan University of Technology and Isfahan University of Technology

detail.title: A Regulatory-Driven Planning Framework for Fast Charging Station Deployment in Power Distribution Systems
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a regulatory-driven planning framework for the optimal deployment of fast charging stations (FCSs) in power distribution systems. In this framework, the regulator incentivizes the distribution system operator (DSO) to enhance two key technical metrics: system reliability under N-1 contingencies and peak-shaving performance under normal state, through collaboration with the FCS aggregator enabled by coordinated vehicle-to-grid (V2G) and grid-to-vehicle (G2V) services. To accomplish this goal, a four-step planning process is proposed. Initially, the baseline FCS planning is determined by the aggregator. Subsequently, the regulator establishes well-structured regulatory mechanisms, including a penalty-reward model (PRM) to promote system reliability and a reward model (RM) to enhance peak-shaving performance. Next, the baseline objective functions of the DSO and FCS aggregator are identified to evaluate their economic interactions. Finally, a system-oriented FCS planning model is formulated as a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) problem that captures the interdependent interactions between both entities, wherein their objectives are jointly optimized under uncertainty in traffic flow and consumers’ demand. Simulation results on the IEEE 33-bus test system verify the effectiveness of the proposed framework in enhancing not only the economic performance of the DSO and FCS aggregator but also the system’s reliability and peak-shaving capability, demonstrating its potential as a practical win-win mechanism for both entities.

title: Breaking the Vicious Circle of Informality in Entrepreneurship: A Conceptual Framework and Policy Agenda

detail.title: Breaking the Vicious Circle of Informality in Entrepreneurship: A Conceptual Framework and Policy Agenda

declarations.ethicsApproval: Only publicly available information has been used.

detail.abstract: While existing research documents barriers facing informal entrepreneurs, it treats these largely as independent constraints. This paper reconceptualizes informality as a self-reinforcing system-a vicious circle where the conditions created by informal status make escape progressively more difficult. Extending Nurkse's (1952) macro-level vicious circle of poverty to the micro level of individual entrepreneurs, this conceptual framework identifies three interlocking feedback loops: financial exclusion (lack of documentation prevents credit access, which prevents formalization), human capital traps (informal work depletes resources needed for skill acquisition), and legitimacy deficits (informal status generates exclusion from formal networks and markets). Drawing on resource-based theory and institutional economics, the framework explains why informal entrepreneurs remain informal despite documented disadvantages-a persistence puzzle existing research cannot adequately address. Three lock-in mechanisms operate simultaneously: the documentation paradox (need credit to formalize, need formalization to access credit), threshold traps (fixed formalization costs exceed variable informal earnings), and capability constraints (lacking bridging social capital to navigate bureaucracy). The framework reveals why piecemeal interventions fail: addressing single barriers leaves other feedback loops active. This reconceptualization has direct policy implications, requiring simultaneous, coordinated interventions across five pillars: tailored finance access, education and training, institutional simplification, social network strengthening, and digital empowerment. Breaking these feedback loops addresses not only resource constraints but also legitimacy deficits, enabling transitions from informality that foster social mobility, gender equity, and sustainable development. This framework-building exercise provides foundations for future empirical validation and guides design of multi-actor interventions for disrupting persistent informality in emerging economies.

title: Will Machines Take Over? Algorithms for Human-Machine Collaborative Decision Making in Healthcare
affiliations: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign - Department of Business Administration, University of Texas at Dallas - Naveen Jindal School of Management and Jindal School of Management - The University of Texas at Dallas

detail.title: Will Machines Take Over? Algorithms for Human-Machine Collaborative Decision Making in Healthcare

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts of interest to report.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Our study did not involve identifiable patient information. The data consisted solely of de-identified imaging predictions and radiologist assessments. Because no identifiable human subject data were used, formal ethics approval was not required.

detail.abstract: Despite significant advancements in predictive artificial intelligence (AI), organizations continue to grapple with determining the most effective integration of AI into their operations, particularly in combining AI with human capabilities in task execution. This paper introduces a diagnostic system aimed at minimizing costs while maintaining patient safety in hospitals by efficiently allocating mammography interpretation tasks between AI algorithms and radiologists. The optimal diagnostic system employs algorithm-generated risk scores for mammograms to determine if additional assessment by a radiologist is necessary. It evaluates the costs of two approaches-automation, where AI completely replaces human interpretation, and delegation, where AI and radiologists share interpretation taskscompared to the current expert-alone strategy. When AI performance does not exceed that of radiologists, the optimal design is a simple two-threshold policy: AI recommends no follow-up for low-risk cases, recommends follow-up for high-risk cases, and delegates ambiguous cases in between to radiologists; the thresholds are analytically derived and state-independent. This two-threshold policy is state-independent and that optimal thresholds are not contingent on the diagnostic system's prior history. We demonstrate our system's performance by back-testing against real-life scenarios, utilizing data from a mammography AI contest and real-world cost and performance metrics. Backtesting demonstrates potential cost savings of up to 20.9% compared to the expert-alone approach. Beyond radiology imaging, our work holds significant implications for the design of workflows in the AI era and human-machine collaboration contexts.

title: Predicting Tariff Decisions from Oral Argument Transcripts with AI Models
affiliations: University of Akron - The George W. Daverio School of Accountancy

detail.title: Predicting Tariff Decisions from Oral Argument Transcripts with AI Models
detail.abstract: This Article uses a single Supreme Court tariffs case as a case study to explore how large language models (LLMs) interpret oral argument and predict case outcomes. The goal is to observe how different LLMs process the same argument transcript, how they translate questioning patterns into probabilistic forecasts, and what these outputs reveal about the models’ implicit picture of judicial reasoning. By limiting the AI models to the argument transcript only, this project seeks to explore how different LLMs would predict the Supreme Court’s decision on a legally and economically significant tariffs dispute and will later assess how those predictions align with the opinion the Court ultimately issues.

title: Winning and Losing Export Sectors of the State Partnership Program
affiliations: Florida International University (FIU) - Department of Economics

detail.title: Winning and Losing Export Sectors of the State Partnership Program
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of the United States Department of War's State Partnership Program (SPP) on state-level sectoral exports. Utilizing a comprehensive sectoral dataset covering the years 2009 to 2024 and employing a Poisson Pseudo-Maximum Likelihood estimation strategy with high-dimensional fixed effects, we analyze whether these security cooperation relationships generate positive spillovers for sector-level state exports. The results suggest that the SPP acts as a significant catalyst for exports in sectors such as animal production, footwear manufacturing, and railroad rolling stock, but it is associated with a decline in exports for sectors like logging, aluminum production, and glass manufacturing. This divergence can be attributed to the SPP's reliance on subject matter expert exchanges to foster comparative advantage in knowledge-intensive sectors by lowering coordination costs, while offering no material benefit to capital-intensive heavy industries. These findings highlight the complex, sector-specific economic dimension of security partnerships and offer crucial insights into the distributional consequences of defense diplomacy.

title: Digitally Inclined Small Businesses: Effects of E-Commerce on Small Business Credit
affiliations: Emory University - Goizueta Business School and Emory University, Goizueta Business School, Students

detail.title: Digitally Inclined Small Businesses: Effects of E-Commerce on Small Business Credit

declarations.funderStatement: Tetyana Balyuk acknowledges the financial support provided by a research grant from Goizueta Business School of Emory University.

detail.abstract: We study how e-commerce affects credit provided to small businesses in the U.S. Theoretical predictions are ambiguous as e-commerce can affect credit supply and demand in opposite directions. We find that small businesses have higher sales, larger orders, and more stable revenue after e-commerce adoption, suggesting that online sales are more efficient than offline trade. Lower cash flow volatility should reduce credit demand, because small businesses often borrow to finance liquidity shortfalls. Yet, we find that businesses obtain more credit after e-commerce adoption, even after controlling for higher efficiency. We confirm these findings using the staggered entry of Uber Eats in the food industry and other strategies. Our results are consistent with e-commerce relieving credit constraints both directly by increasing expected payoffs to lenders due to higher sales and indirectly by lowering lending costs due to hard data generated in e-commerce. We also find redistributional effects of e-commerce on credit across industries in local credit markets.

title: Entropy-Based Allocation & Macro Scenarios

detail.title: Entropy-Based Allocation & Macro Scenarios

contentType.other: Is a research thesis that proposes an investment strategy and new allocation methods.

detail.abstract:
The Diversification Across Macroeconomic Scenarios (DAMS) framework is a new paradigm for understanding asset returns and portfolio construction. It interprets asset allocation through the lens of macroeconomic exposure, arguing that asset prices can be largely explained by variations in the expectations of key macroeconomic variables, namely growth, inflation, and risk premium scenarios. It measures diversification across asset classes, identifying combinations of assets that perform differently depending on whether growth and inflation are rising or falling, as well as the state of the global risk premium.  It is about understanding the fundamental sources of risk and ensuring balance across the underlying economic scenarios that drive asset returns. The integration of DAMS and entropy-based methods offers a unified framework for navigating this complexity, one that aims not to predict markets but to remain prepared for whatever macroeconomic scenario unfolds. In this thesis, we:
- Propose some new allocation methods and study them
- Develop a systematic investment strategy that leverages entropy-based allocation and the DAMS framework.

title: Network Attrition: Theory and Policy Implications
affiliations: Virginia Tech - Department of Economics, Virginia Tech - Department of Economics, Virginia Tech and Virginia Tech - Department of Economics

detail.title: Network Attrition: Theory and Policy Implications
detail.abstract: Networks frequently experience attrition as individual members exit over time. Such departures can significantly impact the behavior of their peers and have cascading effects on overall network activity. We investigate such effects within the framework of the canonical linear-quadratic model of peer influence. We introduce an exogenous shock that removes certain agents from the network, with the key feature that only their immediate neighbors observe these departures. In this setting of incomplete information, we characterize the equilibrium behavior using the Bonacich centrality defined over the belief structures of the agents. We propose the concept of an agent's expected marginal contribution, quantifying the impact of their presence or absence on aggregate network activity. This metric has direct policy relevance: it enables a planner to identify strategically important agents for targeted intervention: either to preserve their participation and enhance collective effort, or to remove them to reduce activity.

title: Dewey Against Parfit on the Trolley Problem: "So what?" The Continuum of Inquiry Trumps Moral Mathematics
affiliations: George Washington University

detail.title: Dewey Against Parfit on the Trolley Problem: "So what?" The Continuum of Inquiry Trumps Moral Mathematics
detail.abstract: Derek Parfit's  1984 work, Reasons and Persons, follows a well-worn path of analytical moral philosophy: formal utilitarian analysis grounded in an immediate view of the universe. Reasons and Persons is replete with examples similar to the famous trolley problem (see 170-184) where we confront the choice of letting a runaway trolley kill several individuals or diverting it into a track where it will kill only one. Parfit shows how easily we can imagine situations of uncertainty in which there is no clear moral message. Parfit's "moral mathematics" explores instances of uncertainty arising in an immediate and instantaneous context. For John Dewey, normative certainty derives not from such constructed puzzles but from experience, which is not revealed in one unique situation but rather from perceptions recognized in many instances over time. Successive instances reveal similarities of practice and of potential therapeutic responses. Dewey's answer to the trolley problem is, perhaps, a banal "So what?" Surely, early instances of a problem often appear unresolvable. Actual trolleys, though, are subject to preventative practices based on actual situations and dangers, avoiding the unlikely trolley dilemma in real life. Dewey's pragmatism investigates how such dilemmas are avoided through the often tenuous path from uncertainty to stable belief and principle. The trolley problem is a dilemma characteristic of analytical moral theory, a constructed situation pitting the value of an individual's life against another's responsibility. Pragmatism's response lies in understanding the transformative nature of a social context of continuous inquiry. The actual continuum is unrecognized in the analysis of hypothetical dilemmas, like the trolley problem, but can clearly be seen in studies of problem resolution in law. Although "reproductive rights" directly conflict in the abstract with "rights to life," the two are repeatedly reconciled in the legal resolution of specific cases. Real moral dilemmas represent actual conflicts, the solution of which cannot be addressed through the analysis of cleverly balanced moral puzzles. Recurring real problems drive the formation and revision of social practices and the predication of general moral rules and principles. Long-standing antinomies in legal theory, like the realist/formalist dichotomy, mirror analogous standoffs presented by Frances Kamm's trolley dilemma and Jonathan Dancy's particularism. The trolley problem defies a Deweyan naturalizing, because it is designed in denial of the normal process of induction regarding actual social problems. Thus, as a purely analytical example, Jonathan Dancy's particularism ignores the hidden inductive history of his "salient" norms, factors that he concedes already exist in an essentially particularist world, and that hide their actual previous Deweyan origins. Dancy ignores the place or stage of uncertainty over particulars that Dewey posits in the developing resolution of actual problems. Dewey opens up and examines the process of ethical inquiry in which particulars are continuously compared and similarities revealed, as remedial practices are adopted and revised to address ethical dilemmas. It is a process that can be called a "shaping;" ethical particularism holds that the evaluative cannot be "cashed out" propositionally, in a context that, according to Dancy, is descriptively "shapeless." Real moral problems at first encounter what may appear to be a "shapeless" particularist context of seemingly unlimited

title: Forecasting College Student Retention: Identifying Selected Factors in Southeastern College
affiliations: University of Pasay, University of Pasay, University of Pasay, University of Pasay and Technological University of the Philippines

detail.title: Forecasting College Student Retention: Identifying Selected Factors in Southeastern College
detail.abstract: This study utilized the quantitative descriptive research to determine the college students' retention in Southeastern College, Pasay City. The respondents of this study were composed of 160 students from the three College Departments at the Southeastern College, Pasay City. This includes students from the different programs offered by the school from 1st year to 4th year level. It was found that the age distribution may have implications for student retention strategies, as younger students may exhibit different academic needs, motivational factors, and levels of independence compared to their older counterparts. While the institution primarily serves middle-income families, there is still a notable proportion of students from both ends of the economic spectrum, underscoring the importance of inclusive policies and financial assistance programs to support retention across all income groups. The regression analysis reveals nuanced enrollment trends in Southeastern College. While student retention remains strong, the observed decline in total enrollment emphasizes the importance of strategic interventions to sustain and improve retention rates across all programs, ensuring that students continue to be supported throughout their academic careers in Southeastern College. The institution should provide academic counseling and peer mentoring programs to help students overcome challenges related to academic adjustment, study habits, and social networks. It is also recommended to expand financial aid options, such as scholarships, grants, and emergency funds, to help alleviate the financial burden and ensure that students can continue their studies without interruption.

title: A Millennium of UK Business Cycles: Insights from Structural VAR Analysis
affiliations: Brazilian Central Bank, Queen Mary, University of London and Bank for International Settlements (BIS)

detail.title: A Millennium of UK Business Cycles: Insights from Structural VAR Analysis
detail.abstract: We study macroeconomic fluctuations in the United Kingdom over seven centuries (1271-2022) using a time-varying VAR with stochastic volatility. We identify business cycle shocks as innovations explaining the largest share of future output variance. Before 1900, these shocks display a stagflationary, supply-driven pattern, while post-1900 shocks become demand-driven, raising both output and inflation. Output volatility declines over time, peaking in the seventeenth century. Monetisation had large real effects in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, shifting to more inflationary impacts thereafter. Our results highlight how business cycle dynamics evolve with institutional, monetary, and structural transformations.

title: When Banks Fail: Depositor Attention and the Cost of Funding for Survivors
affiliations: Emory University - Goizueta Business School and

detail.title: When Banks Fail: Depositor Attention and the Cost of Funding for Survivors
detail.abstract: We document a novel channel through which bank failures affect the economy by increasing the funding costs of surviving banks, thereby further contracting bank credit provision. Using a sample of U.S. bank failures, we find that competitor banks significantly raise deposit rates following a nearby bank failure, even when controlling for local economic conditions and bank fundamentals. The effect is persistent, lasting up to three years, and is stronger following highly publicized failures. At the same time, we observe weaker deposit and loan growth at surviving banks after failures, despite non-bank lending growing in those areas. Consistent with an increase in depositor price sensitivity, we observe price effects for uninsured and insured deposits. Our findings highlight how banking crises propagate indirectly by making funding more expensive, even if remaining banks are safe, thereby constraining credit supply and amplifying economic downturns.

title: AI as a Co-Reflective Extracorporeal Cognitive Organ

detail.title: AI as a Co-Reflective Extracorporeal Cognitive Organ
detail.abstract:
Three-brain thinking refers to the extension of the human cerebro-cerebellar architecture through the incorporation of advanced artificial intelligence. Large language models (LLMs) now function as extracorporeal cognitive systems, enabling the external organisation, transformation and refinement of linguistic and conceptual content. In this functional role, they constitute cognitive organs in the extended-mind sense: non-biological, but capable of supporting reflection and semantic processing outside the skull.
As of 2025, LLMs possess sufficient semantic competence to engage in co-reflective dialogue, allowing the recursive refinement of ideas through structured human–machine interaction. This represents the emergence of a third cognitive locus, complementing cerebral deliberation and cerebellar procedural optimisation.
This transition has implications for cognitive science, suggesting that human cognition may increasingly operate across distributed biological and machine-based processes. It also signals a new class of human–AI integration, in which reflective capability becomes a shared, externally supported cognitive function. This paper introduces and defines that framework.

title: Hilbert Spaces and Narrative Economics: A Formal Operator-Theoretic Framework for Story-Driven Macroeconomic Dynamics
affiliations: Comillas Pontifical University - Faculty of Economics and Business Administration

detail.title: Hilbert Spaces and Narrative Economics: A Formal Operator-Theoretic Framework for Story-Driven Macroeconomic Dynamics
detail.abstract: Narratives shape beliefs, influence expectations, propagate through populations, and affect macroeconomic dynamics. Behavioral economics has documented systematic deviations from rationality, while narrative economics emphasizes that stories spread epidemically and move asset prices, consumption, investment, and policy. This paper develops a rigorous mathematical framework integrating these insights using Hilbert-space methods and operator theory. Beliefs and narratives are represented as vectors in a complete inner-product space; propagation, distortion, and contagion are modeled by linear and nonlinear operators; and macroeconomic expectations emerge as projections of narrative vectors onto relevant economic directions. We derive conditions for viral amplification, exponential forgetting, the existence and uniqueness of stationary narrative states, and the stability of narrative-driven inflation and output expectations. Behavioral distortions such as availability, anchoring, and herding are formalized as nonlinear perturbations. The framework provides a unified structure for incorporating narratives into modern macroeconomic theory without abandoning mathematical rigor.

title: Energy Mix, Diversification and Electricity Price Stability in the European Union, 2010-2025
affiliations: Cracow University of Economics, Centre for Security Studies and Cracow Univeristy of Economics

detail.title: Energy Mix, Diversification and Electricity Price Stability in the European Union, 2010-2025
detail.abstract: This paper examines the influence of the electricity generation mix on wholesale and retail price levels and volatility in the EU-27 from 2010 to 2025. A fixed-effects panel model evaluates renewable energy sources, reliance on fossil fuels, portfolio diversification, EUA carbon prices, gas storage capacities, and EU balancing platforms (PICASSO, MARI).The results confirm the meritorder effect: each extra percentage point of RES lowers wholesale prices by 0.25 EUR/MWh. High HHI and reliance on fossil fuels make prices much more volatile. For example, a 10-point HHI rise raises the price standard deviation by 0.7 EUR/MWh. Higher EUA prices raise prices at both the wholesale and retail levels. Gas storage and cross-border balancing do a lot to reduce volatility, which helps protect against fossil fuel exposure and RES intermittency.Countries with more than 50% RES have prices that are about 40 EUR/MWh lower and half as volatile as those with less than 20% RES. Having a mix of investments and a nuclear or hydro baseload makes things more stable.Just expanding RES won't make sure that things are affordable and safe. For REPowerEU and Fit for 55 to work, we need to diversify, store, price carbon, and integrate the market. Policymakers should put dynamic pricing, demand response, and interconnections at the top of their list of things to do.This is the first long-term study across the EU that looks at how RES penetration, fossil fuel dependence, HHI diversification, and gas storage affect prices and price volatility from the end of the crisis to 2025.

title: Central Bank Digital Currency, Tax Evasion, and Monetary Policy with Heterogeneous Agents
affiliations: University of Hawaii at Manoa and University of Hawaii at Manoa

detail.title: Central Bank Digital Currency, Tax Evasion, and Monetary Policy with Heterogeneous Agents
detail.abstract: We investigate the effects of central bank digital currency (CBDC) issuance in an economy where individuals can evade taxes by using cash. Our tractable model features agent heterogeneity with unobservable idiosyncratic shocks and voluntary exchange, where CBDC and cash compete as payment methods. CBDC's transparency enables governments to collect a labor tax that proves non-distortionary in our quasi-linear environment. Agents with higher marginal utility voluntarily pay fixed fees to access interest-bearing CBDC when their debt constraints bind, allowing the implementation of optimal policy with strictly positive inflation and nominal interest rates. We demonstrate how CBDC enables redistribution between agent types that is not possible in cash-only economies. We conjecture that an optimal CBDC policy involves higher nominal interest rates and lower inflation compared to cash regimes. By reducing tax evasion incentives, the introduction of CBDC can increase both output and aggregate welfare.

title: Traumatic Shocks, Near-Misses, and Radical Innovation
affiliations: Boston University - Questrom School of Business

detail.title: Traumatic Shocks, Near-Misses, and Radical Innovation
detail.abstract: This study examines how direct exposure to traumatic shocks shapes the trajectory and composition of local inventive activity in the United States from 1995 to 2022. Using geolocated U.S. patents and sudden naturaldisaster footprints (1995-2022) in a boundary design with staggered difference-indifferences , the results reveal a distinct post-shock divergence in radical innovation among locations directly affected, those nearly missing the disaster, and those never exposed. Affected locations increase their rate of exploratory innovation by approximately 41% in new technological entries and 29% in innovation novelty compared to near-miss locations, while these same hit areas outperform never-exposed controls by 124% and 22% on the respective measures. In contrast, near-miss locations show a 17% drop in new entries and a 12% decline in novelty versus never-exposed areas. These effects are strongest three to six years post-disaster and attenuated in severe-disaster zones, suggesting a recalibrated willingness to take inventive risks that is bounded by local capacity constraints. Additional analyses show that increased exploration extends beyond disaster-relevant technologies and is not driven by economic rebounds or selective migration. This study contributes new evidence to the behavioral foundations of innovation under uncertainty and underscores the spatial and, often, serendipitous nature of strategic search after trauma.

title: Spatial Media Competition under Multi-Homing

detail.title: Spatial Media Competition under Multi-Homing
detail.abstract: Two media outlets spatially compete to report an issue in the presence of multi-homing readers who read both outlets' reports. I propose a one-dimensional perception index which shows that perception of an outlet's report varies not only across single and multi-homing readers, but also within multi-homing readers, based on their sequence of reading both outlets' reports. I apply this index to examine how outlets with opposing ideological goals strategically acquire (via investment) and reveal (via spin) information after weighing their own ideological objectives against reader perception concerns. I find that when reporting an ideologically neutral issue, outlets coordinate investment and spin to piggy-back on each other's reports. However, when reporting ideologically non-neutral issues, coordination ceases ---  outlets not only spin to counter its competitor's report, but by strategic investment also abstains from acquiring information that favors their position, thereby impeding its competitor from piggy-backing with countering information.

title: A Preferred-Habitat Model of Term Structure with Dealer Market Power
affiliations: University of British Columbia (UBC) - Sauder School of Business

detail.title: A Preferred-Habitat Model of Term Structure with Dealer Market Power
detail.abstract: The repo market finances approximately 70% of U.S. Treasury holdings. Recent evidence documents substantial dealer market power in this market. This paper examines how this market power shapes the term structure of interest rates and monetary policy transmission. I develop a preferredhabitat model in which dealers monopolistically compete for short-term funding to finance carry trades in long-term bonds. Market power in the funding market enables dealers to strategically restrict their carry positions and extract higher spreads between bond returns and funding costs, thereby generating elevated bond risk premia. I show analytically that this mechanism amplifies the sensitivity of risk premia to the yield curve slope and strengthens the transmission of monetary policy shocks to long-term yields. Empirically, I construct a measure of dealer market power using the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) of repo borrowing concentration from money market funds. Consistent with the model's predictions, higher repo market concentration is positively associated with elevated term premia (both in ex-ante expectations and in ex-post realized bond returns), larger Fama-Bliss coefficients, and greater sensitivity of long-term yields to short-rate shocks. These findings reveal that dealer market power in the repo market plays a crucial role in shaping bond risk premia and the transmission of monetary policy through the yield curve.

title: Fiscal Event Geometry and the Two-Axis Fiscal Framework: A Coordinated Approach to Institutional Tension
affiliations: Ontario Institute for Studies in Education (OISE), University of Toronto

detail.title: Fiscal Event Geometry and the Two-Axis Fiscal Framework: A Coordinated Approach to Institutional Tension

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This conceptual study did not involve human participants and therefore did not require ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
This paper develops Fiscal Event Geometry, a coordinate-based framework for representing how tax, migration, education, and intergenerational wealth systems generate observable fiscal events. The model formalizes institutions as state spaces defined by two underlying dimensions: cross-jurisdictional fiscal position and intergenerational carrying capacity. Within this space, rule-based fiscal events—such as disclosures, boundary checks, capital transfers, or verification triggers—produce trajectories, densities, and discontinuities that can be studied as geometric objects rather than narrative categories.

The framework proposes a data-generating process (DGP) in which institutional rules initiate events, events update coordinates, and the resulting point cloud exhibits structural properties suitable for econometric modeling. This working paper outlines the theoretical architecture, the geometry of fiscal movement, and the methodological implications for analyzing institutional tension and rule-driven inequality. Technical estimators and index construction details are presented separately in forthcoming work.

title: How Local Economies Recover from Manufacturing Job Loss: The Case of China Shock
affiliations: National University of Singapore

detail.title: How Local Economies Recover from Manufacturing Job Loss: The Case of China Shock
detail.abstract: This paper argues that local higher education institutions played a central role in local recovery from China import exposure. More exposed regions host more universities and experienced faster enrollment growth, which stimulated employment through two channels: (1) a demand channel, in which rising student spending boosts local markets for education and nontradables, and (2) a supply channel, in which students remain to work locally after acquiring human capital. Out-of-state and foreign students primarily drive the demand channel, underscoring the role of trade in services in local recovery. In contrast, two-thirds of the supply channel functions by enhancing human capital acquisition of in-state residence, with the remaining one-third through attracting students elsewhere and retaining them locally.
